Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation
[MATH: \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
We can immediately calculate a solution, called the principal value, as follows:
[MATH: x = \arccos\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 30^\circ]

Content:
Since [MATH: 30^\circ] lies inside the required domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1=30^\circ.] This angle lies in the first quadrant and has reference angle [MATH: \theta_R=30^\circ.]

Content:
But there is another solution. Since [MATH: \cos x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} >0,] the second solution to the equation will lie in the fourth quadrant, and its reference angle is also [MATH: \theta_R=30^\circ.] To find the second solution, we use a CAST diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5750863898c40dc5746ff22c72985508]

Content:
Since the second solution [MATH: x_2] lies in the [MATH: 4]th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x_{2}|= 360^{∘} − θ_{R}; = 360^{∘} − 30^{∘}; = 330^{∘}]

Content:
So, the solutions are [MATH: x=30^\circ, 330^\circ.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 2\cos{x}+\sqrt{2}=0] for [MATH: 0 \leq x < 2\pi.]
sections.readable_text: Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 2\cos{x}+\sqrt{2}=0] for [MATH: 0 \leq x < 2\pi.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating [MATH: \cos x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 2\cos x + sqrt(2)|= 0; 2\cos x|= − sqrt(2); \cos x|= − (sqrt(2))/(2)]

Now, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arccos (− (sqrt(2))/(2)) = (3π)/(4)]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{4}] lies inside the specified domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.]

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of [MATH: \theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.] Since [MATH: \cos{x} < 0,] the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle [MATH: \theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]

Since the second solution [MATH: x_2] lies in the [MATH: 3]rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

[MATH: x_{2}|= π + θ_{R}; = π + (π)/(4); = (5π)/(4)]

So, the solutions are [MATH: x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation
[MATH: \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
We can immediately calculate a solution, called the principal value, as follows:
[MATH: x = \arccos\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 30^\circ]

Content:
Since [MATH: 30^\circ] lies inside the required domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1=30^\circ.] This angle lies in the first quadrant and has reference angle [MATH: \theta_R=30^\circ.]

Content:
But there is another solution. Since [MATH: \cos x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} >0,] the second solution to the equation will lie in the fourth quadrant, and its reference angle is also [MATH: \theta_R=30^\circ.] To find the second solution, we use a CAST diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5750863898c40dc5746ff22c72985508]

Content:
Since the second solution [MATH: x_2] lies in the [MATH: 4]th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x_{2}|= 360^{∘} − θ_{R}; = 360^{∘} − 30^{∘}; = 330^{∘}]

Content:
So, the solutions are [MATH: x=30^\circ, 330^\circ.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Cosine with Special Angles

Example Prompt:
Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 2\cos{x}+\sqrt{2}=0] for [MATH: 0 \leq x < 2\pi.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating [MATH: \cos x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 2\cos x + sqrt(2)|= 0; 2\cos x|= − sqrt(2); \cos x|= − (sqrt(2))/(2)]

Now, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arccos (− (sqrt(2))/(2)) = (3π)/(4)]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{4}] lies inside the specified domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.]

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of [MATH: \theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.] Since [MATH: \cos{x} < 0,] the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle [MATH: \theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]

[IMG: /graphics/03de6ea8bbd2a7d0c85d8e4354af305d]

Since the second solution [MATH: x_2] lies in the [MATH: 3]rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

[MATH: x_{2}|= π + θ_{R}; = π + (π)/(4); = (5π)/(4)]

So, the solutions are [MATH: x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}.]

Since [MATH: 0.644] lies inside the given domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 = 0.644.]

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of [MATH: \theta_R = 0.644.] Since [MATH: \cos{x} > 0,] the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle [MATH: \theta_R = 0.644.]

[MATH: x_{2}|= 2π − θ_{R}; = 2π − 0.644; = 5.639]

So, the solutions (rounded to one decimal place) are [MATH: x = 0.6, 5.6.]
